topic: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
parentTitle: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
title: Child and adolescent mental health
blurb: Apply the right consent rules at each age, follow NICE NG134 for depression in young people and plan transition to adult services.
question: Ellie, 17, has severe depression and has capacity. The team recommends informal admission to an adolescent unit. Ellie agrees, but her father refuses and says she is still a child. What is the legal position?

teach.body: Child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) care for people under 18. The illnesses overlap with adults' (depression, anxiety, self-harm, eating disorders, psychosis), but consent, treatment choices and safeguards differ by age. Plain English: always ask two questions first, 'How old are they?' and 'Can they make this decision?', because the answer changes who decides.
teach.cite: MCA 2005 s2(5); MHA 1983 s131; Gillick v West Norfolk [1986]

teach.h: Who can consent to mental health care?
teach.caption: MHA s131(2)-(5): for 16-17s, capacity is judged under the MCA, and a capable young person's consent or refusal of informal admission stands whatever a parent says.

head: Rule
Detail
rows: Every year if no hearing (3 years for adults)
SOAD needed even if the young person consents
teach.caption: MHA 2025 s52, in force from 6 April 2026, requires the Secretary of State to review whether CQC notification duties should cover more under-18 admissions; most 2025 Act changes are not yet in force.

teach.h: NG134: depression in children and young people

steps.label: Still mild after 2 weeks
steps.sub: Digital CBT, group CBT or group IPT

teach.caption: NG134 1.5.1, 1.5.7, 1.6.10. No antidepressant for initial treatment of mild depression (1.5.3).

Second line: sertraline or citalopram (1.6.22). Paroxetine, venlafaxine and tricyclics are not used (1.6.26-1.6.27). Monitor closely for suicidal behaviour, self-harm or hostility, especially early on (NG134 1.6.18).

teach.h: Self-harm and safety in young people
items: Under-18s who self-harm should be assessed by a professional experienced in working with children and young people (NG225).
Consider DBT for adolescents (DBT-A) for frequent self-harm with significant emotional dysregulation (NG225).
Warn the young person and parents to make urgent contact if new suicidal thoughts, self-harm or hostility appear on an antidepressant.
Think safeguarding at every contact: a young person's distress may reflect harm at home or online.

items.label: Start planning for adulthood at the latest
Transfer at a stable time, not a fixed birthday

teach.caption: NG43 1.2.1, 1.2.3: no rigid age threshold; plan transfer at a time of relative stability.

teach.body: Ellie is 17, so her capacity is judged under the Mental Capacity Act, and she has capacity. Under s131 of the Mental Health Act her consent to informal admission is enough, even though her father objects. The nurse explains this calmly to her father, involves him as far as Ellie agrees, and makes sure the unit is age-appropriate. If Ellie had refused, her father could not have consented to admission on her behalf.

teach.text: Gillick is for UNDER-16s. For 16-17-year-olds the test for informal admission is MCA capacity (s131(5)), not Gillick. And a capable 16-17-year-old's refusal of informal admission cannot be overridden by a parent: if admission is needed, the MHA is considered instead.

items: Under 16: Gillick competence. 16-17: MCA capacity; s131 lets a capable young person decide on informal admission.
No police station as a place of safety for under-18s; annual tribunal referral; SOAD for ECT even with consent.
NG134: watchful waiting then psychological therapy; fluoxetine is the first antidepressant if needed, 10 mg start.
Transition planning from year 9 at the latest; transfer at a stable time.

summary: You can now apply Gillick, the MCA and s131 to decide who consents to care for a young person, and list the MHA safeguards special to under-18s. You can also follow NG134 for depression, including fluoxetine, and plan transition under NG43.

A.q: Which antidepressant does NICE NG134 recommend when medication is needed for moderate to severe depression in a 15-year-old?
options: Sertraline
Paroxetine
Fluoxetine
Venlafaxine
A.why: NG134: if an antidepressant is prescribed for a child or young person, it should be fluoxetine, the only one where trial evidence shows benefits outweigh risks.

whyNot.0: Sertraline is second line after fluoxetine has failed or is not tolerated.
whyNot.1: NG134: paroxetine should not be used for depression in young people.
whyNot.3: NG134: venlafaxine should not be used for depression in young people.

A.q: A 14-year-old is detained under section 136 in a shopping centre. Where may the police NOT take her as a place of safety?
options: A hospital-based place of safety
A police station
An emergency department
A residential care home
A.why: MHA s136A(1): a person under 18 may not be removed to, kept at or taken to a police station as a place of safety.

whyNot.0: A health-based place of safety is the expected choice.
whyNot.2: An emergency department can be used as a place of safety.
whyNot.3: Any suitable place whose occupier agrees can be a place of safety; the bar is on police stations for under-18s.

A.q: Which test decides whether a 13-year-old can consent to talking therapy without her parents' agreement?
options: Gillick competence
The Mental Capacity Act test
The s131 informal admission test
The Fraser guidelines on contraception
A.why: For under-16s, the test is Gillick competence: enough understanding and intelligence to understand fully what is proposed.

whyNot.3: The Fraser guidelines concern contraceptive advice specifically.

B.q: Jamal, 16, has capacity and refuses informal admission to an adolescent unit. His mother wants to consent on his behalf. What is the position under the Mental Health Act 1983?
options: His mother's consent is sufficient for admission
His mother can consent if a court agrees later
His refusal cannot be overridden by parental consent
He can be admitted informally under the MCA
B.why: MHA s131(4): if a capable 16-17-year-old does not consent, informal admission cannot be based on the consent of a person with parental responsibility.

whyNot.0: s131(4) prevents parental consent overriding his refusal.
whyNot.1: There is no retrospective court route for this informal admission.
whyNot.3: A capable person refusing admission cannot be admitted under the MCA.

B.q: Maya, 14, has mild depression and does not want treatment right now. What does NICE NG134 advise?
options: Start fluoxetine 10 mg daily
Discharge with advice to return if worse
Refer for inpatient assessment
Watchful waiting with review within 2 weeks
B.why: NG134 1.5.1: for mild depression where the young person does not want an intervention, arrange further assessment, normally within 2 weeks (watchful waiting).

whyNot.0: Antidepressants should not be used for initial treatment of mild depression.
whyNot.1: NG134 expects a planned review, not discharge.
whyNot.2: Mild depression does not need inpatient assessment.

B.q: Noah, 15, starts fluoxetine with CBT. What should the nurse tell Noah and his parents?
options: Contact the prescriber urgently if new suicidal thoughts appear
Expect a full response within the first week of treatment
Stop the tablets straight away once he feels better
Double the dose himself if he feels no benefit after 3 days
B.why: NG134 1.6.18: monitor for suicidal behaviour, self-harm or hostility, especially early in treatment; the young person and parents should make urgent contact if these appear.

whyNot.2: NG134 advises continuing for 6 months after remission.
whyNot.3: Doses change only on the prescriber's advice.

C.q: Zara, 17, has been detained under section 3 for 20 months. A tribunal last considered her case 13 months ago and she has not applied since. What must the hospital managers do?
options: Wait until she applies to the tribunal herself
Refer her once 3 years have passed, as for adults
Refer her now, as more than 1 year has passed
Ask her nearest relative to make the referral
C.why: MHA s68(6): managers must refer when more than 3 years (or 1 year if under 18) have passed since the tribunal last considered the case.

whyNot.0: Automatic referral protects patients who do not apply.
whyNot.3: The duty to refer lies with the hospital managers.

C.q: Leo, 16, is competent and agrees to ECT for life-threatening depression on a young people's unit. What is required?
options: His written consent is sufficient
Consent from both parents as well
A court order before each treatment
A certificate from a SOAD as well
C.why: MHA s58A(4): for a patient under 18 who consents to ECT, a SOAD must also certify that he is capable, consents and the treatment is appropriate.

whyNot.0: Under-18s need a SOAD even when consenting.
whyNot.1: Parental consent is not what s58A requires.
whyNot.2: A court order is not required for each treatment.

C.q: Priya, 17, with an eating disorder, is due to move from CAMHS to adult services on her 18th birthday, during a period of rapid weight loss. What does NICE NG43 support?
options: Transfer on her birthday as the service policy states
Transfer at a time of relative stability
Discharge from CAMHS and ask her GP to re-refer
Pause all care until she is medically stable
C.why: NG43 1.2.3: there should be no rigid age threshold; transfer should happen at a time of relative stability, with planning started early.

whyNot.0: A rigid birthday transfer in a crisis is what NG43 advises against.
whyNot.2: Discharge and re-referral creates a gap in care.
whyNot.3: Care continues; only the timing of transfer changes.

reteach.title: Age first, then capacity
reteach.question: How do you work out who decides about a young person's care?

blocks.body: Under 16: is the child Gillick competent for this decision? 16 or 17: does the young person have capacity under the MCA? For informal admission at 16-17, a capable young person's yes or no stands (s131). If admission is needed and refused, the MHA, not a parent, is the route considered.

blocks.text: At 16-17 use the MCA, not Gillick.

explain.body: Under 16: Gillick. 16-17: MCA capacity. A capable 16-17-year-old's consent to, or refusal of, informal admission stands regardless of parents (s131).

test.q: For a 16-year-old's informal admission, how is capacity assessed under section 131(5)?
options: Using Gillick competence
Using the Fraser guidelines
Using the Mental Capacity Act
Using parental opinion
test.why: s131(5)(a): capacity for 16-17-year-olds is read in accordance with the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

explain.body: No police station as a place of safety; tribunal referral after 1 year without a hearing; SOAD for ECT even if consenting; age-appropriate wards.

items.label: police stations as places of safety

test.q: Which statement about under-18s and the Mental Health Act 1983 is correct?
options: A police station can be used if no bed is free
ECT needs no SOAD if a 17-year-old consents
Detention needs both parents' agreement
Tribunal referral is due every 1 year if no hearing
test.why: s68(6): referral after 1 year without a tribunal for under-18s, rather than 3 years.

whyNot.0: s136A bars police stations for under-18s.
whyNot.1: s58A requires a SOAD for consenting under-18s.
whyNot.2: Detention criteria and applications do not require parental agreement.

explain.body: Mild: watchful waiting, then digital or group therapies; no antidepressant first. Moderate to severe: psychological therapy; fluoxetine added after 4-6 sessions without response.

test.q: When does NICE NG134 advise offering fluoxetine to a 13-year-old with moderate depression?
options: At the first appointment, with no therapy
If no response after 4-6 therapy sessions
When inpatient admission is first needed
After 2 weeks of watchful waiting
test.why: NG134 1.6.10: following MDT review, offer fluoxetine if moderate to severe depression in a young person is unresponsive to a specific psychological therapy after 4-6 sessions.

whyNot.2: Fluoxetine is used in community care too.
whyNot.3: Watchful waiting is for mild depression.

explain.body: Plan for adulthood from year 9 (13-14) at the latest; no rigid age cut-off; transfer at a time of relative stability, with a named worker.

test.q: By when does NICE NG43 say planning for adulthood should start at the latest?
options: Year 9, around age 13-14
Age 17, a year before transfer
Six months before the 18th birthday
On the day of the 18th birthday
test.why: NG43 1.2.1: start planning for adulthood from year 9 (13-14) at the latest.

whyNot.1: This is later than NG43 advises.
whyNot.2: Six months is far too late.
